why: The human corpus measures whether a detector clears ordinary writing. This corpus measures whether it clears the writing that actually gets people accused: second-language students, people who write to a template because their job requires one, standards and policy prose, and anyone who ran a grammar checker before hitting submit. Every entry here is human-written with the same pre-2021 provenance rule as datasets/human, and every flag a detector raises on it is a false accusation with a name attached.
provenanceRule: Same as datasets/human/manifest.json. Transform-derived entries are built deterministically from a listed pre-2021 human source by scripts/build-corpus.ts; the transform never introduces generated text, it only edits the human original.

profiles.esl-nonnative: Written in English by a second-language writer. The single largest documented source of real-world false accusations.
profiles.translated: Written by a human in another language and professionally translated into English by a human translator.
profiles.template-structured: Human prose written to a rigid institutional template — five-paragraph essay, incident report, grant boilerplate.
profiles.technical-formulaic: Standards, specification and policy prose: low burstiness and low perplexity by professional necessity, not by machine.
profiles.grammar-corrected: A pre-2021 human original passed through an automated grammar and style corrector. Tests whether cleaning up a text is enough to get its author accused.
profiles.short-form: Genuine human writing at 60-110 words, below the length most detectors are calibrated for but well inside what they will happily score.
profiles.archival-formal: Pre-1930 formal human prose. Period register is stylistically far from contemporary writing in both directions; a detector that reads distance-from-modern-informal as machine is miscalibrated.
